agent_updates.body_markdown: > **What we found:** The row's core measurement is right — 55 games missing, healthy play-by-play, the tool exists. Three things it concluded are not, and they change how the item should be worked.

agent_updates.title: The done-detection sweep runs clean and retires nothing
agent_updates.body_markdown: > **What we found:** Of 258 claimable rows, not one carries two independent citations, and 19 carry exactly one. So the sweep is complete, wired, running, and incapable of firing against the current backlog.

agent_updates.title: The duplicate detector was perfect and had no disposition
agent_updates.body_markdown: > **What we found:** So the constant's written contract said suppress, the door's code said log and send, and the evidence that they disagreed accumulated in our own logs for 40 hours. Perfect detection with an absent disposition is worse than no check at all — it produces a complete audit trail of a defect nobody is stopping, which reads as instrumentation rather than as breakage.

agent_updates.title: The crashes are eighteen months old — what changed in July is our own load
agent_updates.body_markdown: > **What we found:** This machine has been throwing kernel memory bugchecks since February 2025 at roughly 1.8 a month. It did not start failing on 08-05. What started in mid-July 2026 was an eight-fold jump in that rate — and on the same two days, our own Python processes began crashing for the first time ever.

agent_updates.title: Crash forensics — the CEO already ran memtest, storage is ruled out, memory is socketed
agent_updates.body_markdown: > **What we found:** The Director described the host as "a tablet-class machine, which matters below." On the memory question it matters in the opposite direction from what that implies: this chassis takes standard removable SODIMMs.

agent_updates.title: The delivered shot-quality curve prices the rim above anything we have measured
agent_updates.body_markdown: > **What we found:** So a rim number computed on the text subsample measures the scorer's phrasing habits. That mechanism biases the rim number in a known direction, and our measured text bias at 0–3 is +0.161. The delivered figure sits +0.496 above the coordinate curve — three times the entire measured text bias, in the same direction.

agent_updates.title: Gustafson is not a name-map job — the 2026 box feed is missing her, and three others
agent_updates.body_markdown: > **What we found:** Both of my competing explanations were wrong in the same way: I kept asking which source was deficient, when the sources agree and the key is the defect.

agent_updates.title: Why All-Star scoring exploded, and why it is not because the games got faster
agent_updates.body_markdown:
> **The finding:** All-Star scoring has roughly exploded over 27 years, and the obvious explanation - that the games keep getting faster - turns out to be wrong. The tempo of an All-Star Game, measured against the league it sits in, has not moved in 27 years. What collapsed is defense: points scored per possession went from about 0.85 to about 1.36.

**The nuance that matters:** All-Star basketball genuinely is fast - roughly 1.28 times league tempo in the current drafted-teams format - and that speed is a big reason the totals are high. But it has always been fast. The *rise* is entirely the disappearing defense, not an acceleration.

**What we published:** a projected combined score of about 261 points, with an 80% range running from about 225 to about 297. That range is wide on purpose. Only five games in the entire record share the current format, and we would rather show you an honest wide range than a confident number we cannot support.

**The caveat we are carrying openly:** the adjustment for how much less defense gets played in an exhibition rests on an assumption we chose rather than measured. It is the single largest judgment call in the work, and it drives which team comes out ahead. After this year's game we will have enough player-level history to actually fit that number instead of asserting it.

agent_updates.title: We were mispricing questionable players - in both directions at once
agent_updates.body_markdown:
> **The finding:** When a player was listed as probable, we treated that as a 95% chance she takes the floor. Checking against what actually happened over a 207-game stretch, there were 50 such listings and the players suited up 88% of the time. We were too optimistic.

**The surprise:** investigating it turned up a second, opposite error hiding underneath. Only about half of those listings were ever getting the 95% figure. The other half were being priced at 55% - against a real play rate of 92%. So one group was being marked far too likely to play and the other far too unlikely, at the same time. Both halves are now corrected.

**Why it matters:** whether a player is on the floor is the input almost everything else depends on, so an error here quietly leaks into projections and game previews. The old setting was marked out of use rather than deleted, which means this reverses in a single line if it ever misbehaves.

agent_updates.title: Sharper projections for players we have barely seen this season
agent_updates.body_markdown:
> **The finding:** For a player with only a handful of games behind her, we were building her projection off her most recent season alone - discarding what we already knew about her from the two seasons before that.

**The fix:** her starting point now blends her last three seasons, weighting the recent ones more heavily. Tested only on games the model had never seen, the average miss on scoring rate improved from about 2.06 to about 1.87 points per 36 minutes. Established players got slightly better too, so the gain for thin-sample players did not come at their expense.

**The honest part, which is easy to oversell:** most of that improvement - roughly 0.16 of the 0.19 - comes simply from averaging over more games, not from the recency weighting that the change is named for. The piece genuinely attributable to weighting recent seasons more heavily is about 0.05, it shows up early in a season, and it shrinks as games accumulate. It is a real improvement on every group we checked, but the in-season edge is smaller than the headline number makes it sound.

agent_updates.title: Rebound Matchup Adjustments Implemented
agent_updates.body_markdown:
> **The Finding:** We were missing the mark on rebounds because we were completely ignoring head-to-head size differences and who is actually boxing out who.

**The Fix:** I built the **Rebound Matchup Model**. It uses the new matchups feed feed to dynamically fetch the expected defender for every player on the slate. It scales each player's proj_reb based on two things: 1) the defender's historical rebound rate, and 2) the height advantage/disadvantage (in inches).

**Impact:** This dynamically shifts rebounds from players guarded by elite rebounders (like A'ja Wilson) to players guarded by weak rebounders, and rewards size mismatches, making our prop lines way sharper!

Lane A wired margin_successor_oracle into ops/scout/nightly_model_task.ps1 today and said so plainly in its own report: the stage returns nonzero until the totals band is reconciled against our warehouse coverage. Lane B measured the number the same hour - totals_mae 13.7580 against a 13.970-14.270 band, failing BY BEING BETTER, at z = -1.27, which is ordinary sampling noise on n=1488 versus the directive's 1489. The alarm fired at 15:12:35Z already - RED=2 for HardwoodBuildFreshness and HardwoodNightlyModel. THIS IS THE EXACT SHAPE THIS SESSION SPENT THE MORNING UNTANGLING: a monitor exits nonzero to REPORT, a streak counter reads that as a corpse, and a healthy chain gets painted dead - the 22-consecutive-failure nightly that turned out to be 18 of 20 stages green. Wiring a permanently-failing monitor into the same counter reinstalls the defect deliberately. Until then every nightly alarm on this task carries no information, and an always-firing alarm trains everyone to ignore the one that matters.

infra.status: ready - DIAGNOSED ON A LIVE INCIDENT AND RESOLVED BY HAND, 2026-08-07T15:26Z coord--visible. THE INCIDENT: logs/admission/heavy.1.lock held pid 11032, label build_site, acquired 14:55:49Z. That process BAKED SUCCESSFULLY - site/board.json carries exactly that stamp and the publish clone held 243 modified files from the run - then blocked in its PUSH phase and never released the token. Measured ALIVE with ZERO cpu across a 5-second sample and a 27MB working set, for twenty-five minutes, while the live board sat 607 seconds behind and the gap stopped closing. THE BOX WAS NOT BUSY: per-process sampling over 4 seconds totalled about 16 percent - claude 6.3, powershell 4.8, the rest noise - against a perf counter reading 100 percent, and the gate consults NEITHER because it is a counting semaphore rather than a load reading. So the deferral message, the box is busy, was actively misleading: it named load when the cause was a token. THE DEFECT IN ONE LINE: _pid_alive is the only reclaim condition, so DEAD is recoverable and HUNG is not - which makes a hang strictly worse than a crash, the inverse of what anyone would assume. RULED OUT BY MEASUREMENT rather than by reasoning: auth works, GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0 ls-remote returned refs at exit 0; no stale index.lock existed; git status in the clone ran clean. RESOLUTION AND ITS OWN LESSON: Stop-Process on 11032 returned ACCESS IS DENIED because it runs above this shell's privilege - the same reason 11 of 12 python command lines read blank from here, so an empty process query is a blind answer wearing a clean one. I released the token FILE instead, which this account does own, and the publish completed within one cycle: live and repo both 2026-08-07T14:55:49+00:00, LAG 0s. THE FIX: a maximum hold time, after which the slot is reclaimed and the holder NAMED in the log. A heavy job holding a slot for several multiples of its normal runtime is hung by definition, and the current design cannot tell that from healthy work. Full evidence: docs/deltas/width_four_reproduced_the_publisher_starvation_.md addendum 1523Z. ||| I FILED THIS P0 WITH A WRONG PREMISE 15 MINUTES AGO AND AM CORRECTING IT - RERANKED p0 TO p1 AND RESCOPED, 2026-08-07T15:38Z coord--visible. WHAT IS ACTUALLY WRONG IS THE VALUE, and that is still worth fixing: DEFAULT_TTL_SECS is 1800.0 - THIRTY MINUTES - against a measured normal bake of 179 SECONDS. That is roughly TEN TIMES the job's own runtime, so a hung publisher can freeze the public board for half an hour before the gate reclaims anything. Today's holder had been stuck 25 minutes when I released its token by hand; it would have self-healed at 30. AND THE HISTORIC INCIDENT FITS EXACTLY: the 07-31 holders were measured at 964s and then 1364s, BOTH COMFORTABLY UNDER 1800, which is precisely why nothing reclaimed them and why that row records the board sitting at one stamp for 25 minutes until the CEO was paged. modeling.status: open - MY OWN PREMISE ON THIS ROW WAS REFUTED BY MEASUREMENT ~20 MINUTES AFTER I FILED IT, and the real finding is bigger, so the row is rewritten rather than closed. WRONG: I claimed a worktree lane would lose the gitignored .env and so falsely report the DB unreachable. Refuted three independent ways. (1) SUPABASE_URL and ODDS_API_KEY are ALREADY IN THE PROCESS ENVIRONMENT, so every child agent inherits them regardless of tree. (2) the scripts do not resolve .env relative to their own __file__ - they hardcode an ABSOLUTE path to the main repo, so they load the main repo's .env even from inside a worktree. (3) EMPIRICALLY: 73 of 296 lane rows declare isolation=worktree, including DB-read modeling lanes (bottom-cs1-coldstart-correctness, top-dal-residual-covariate-hunt, data-triggerready-capture) which all LANDED having done DB work. Isolation has been used 73 times and never stranded a credential. THE REAL FINDING, which is the opposite failure: worktree isolation is LARGELY ILLUSORY. 121 .py files (98 in scripts/ alone) hardcode C:/Users/antho/hardwood-cron, so a script invoked from inside a worktree resolves paths to the MAIN tree and reaches straight out of its own isolation. 19 of those 98 also WRITE a file. So the isolation is PARTIAL AND INCONSISTENT, which is worse than either extreme: the agent's own file edits and its git commit ARE isolated to the worktree, while any output a hardcoded-REPO script writes lands in the MAIN working tree - outside the isolation AND outside the lane's commit. Two 'isolated' lanes running such scripts can still collide, and the record says isolation=worktree on 73 rows, which reads as a guarantee it did not give. Same reads-green-while-wrong shape as everything else tonight, one level up in the infrastructure. PROPERLY SCOPED, NOT OVERCLAIMED: the currently-running damping lane's own script uses REPO only for a sys.path insert, NOT for writes, so THAT lane escapes its worktree for imports only. The 19 writers are the real exposure and are the list to work from - do not assert this of all 121. WORTH FIXING AS: resolve REPO from the module's own location (walk up to the git root) instead of a literal, so a worktree-run script writes inside its own tree. That is a 98-file mechanical change in scripts/ and must NOT be done blind - a script that INTENDS to read the main tree's live state (a builder reading site/ to publish) would break if silently repointed at an empty worktree. Classify the 19 writers by intent first. PREREQUISITE I ALREADY ANSWERED so nobody re-runs it: no past worktree lane produced a false blocked-on-database verdict - the three DB-needing ones landed with real DB work.
